```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The goal is a paying customer within 90 days. B sells to owner-operator contractors through self-serve monthly SaaS at $50–$125/month, with free trials and no procurement process. A sells to municipalities, and A's own brief says RFPs, insurance certificates and cooperative-purchasing vetting make that cycle slow. That is a poor fit for a 90-day first sale.",
    "Willingness to pay at B's price point is backed by sourced, published pricing from several direct competitors: EstimationPro at $66 and $124/month, Outdoor Estimates at $49.99/month, and QuoteIQ from $29.99/month. A small, low-commitment purchase is easier for a solo operator to win than a municipal contract.",
    "B's brief says some competitors (EstimationPro, Outdoor Estimates) were built and run by single contractor-founders. That suggests a one-person, AI-assisted operation can ship and run this kind of product. The brief gives no direct source for the solo-founder claim, though, so it is supporting rather than decisive.",
    "A's urgency rests on a regulatory deadline that has already been extended, to April 2027 and April 2028. That pushes the forcing function well beyond 90 days. A's own Case Against admits further delays or lax enforcement could erode willingness to pay.",
    "A's most valuable layer, legally defensible compliance documentation, carries liability risk that A's brief says a solo, uninsured operator is poorly positioned to absorb. B's regulatory setup is light by comparison: a hosted payment processor for PCI scope and a templated privacy policy.",
    "Both markets are crowded, with five or more competitors each. Crowding does not separate the two, so the decision rests on sales-cycle speed and deal size, where B is stronger."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's demand evidence consists of two quotes from Cole County, MO officials. Neither shows willingness to pay a new vendor. Landwehr's quote shows resentment of the mandate and a tendency to comply by deleting content ('the way to do it is just remove information'). Cole County had also already paid Continual Engine $7,000, so it is a captured buyer rather than an open prospect. The NLC booth-cost figure, which supports A's main acquisition channel, comes from a 2015 prospectus, and the state-league booths cited are already sold out.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. B's own evidence is thin. Only one demand quote is sourced; the second has an unretrieved URL and counts as missing. The $237 cost-per-lead is a generic B2B SaaS benchmark, not a contractor-specific figure. B also enters as roughly the eighth near-identical product, with real accuracy and trust risk. A has better-documented proof of actual spending ($7,000 Cole County, $2,510 Templeton quote). The pick for B rests mainly on fit to the 90-day, one-person constraint (procurement speed, deal size, liability), not on B having stronger demand evidence overall."
}
```
